text: Reading Two · Wheatley, West, Charlton, Sanders, Smith & Taylor (2009) Improving Behavior through Differential Reinforcement: A Praise Note System Abstract Abstract Schools are often in need of low-cost, high-impact strategies to improve student behavior in school common areas. While many behavior management programs exist, there are few resources available to guide the implementation of these programs and ensure they are grounded in evidence-based strategies. Therefore, the current study had two primary purposes: first, to demonstrate the effectiveness of a simple behavior management system, and second, to begin the process of providing some guidance for the application of similar systems. The study used a differential reinforcement of incompatible behavior (DRI) procedure in a multiple-baseline design across three target behaviors to decrease inappropriate and increase appropriate behaviors in an elementary school lunchroom. The intervention consisted of (1) teaching specific appropriate behaviors, (2) providing opportunities for students to practice skills, and (3) implementing a Praise Note system to reward students for behaving appropriately. Students were taught appropriate behaviors, and the school staff was trained to recognize and reward students who kept the lunchroom clean, sat appropriately in their seats, and walked in the lunchroom. Data show significant decreases for each of three target behaviors. The average amount of litter left in the lunchroom decreased by 96%, the average number of instances of sitting inappropriately decreased by 64%, and the average number of instances of running in the lunchroom decreased by 75%. Beyond contributing to the effective intervention strategies available to reduce problem behaviors in common areas, this research also provides much needed guidance for effectively implementing the necessary components of a Praise Note system — namely, program intensity and delivery. Background: behavior in school common areas Behavior problems are a well-documented and ever-increasing challenge facing educators (Mayer, 2001; Walker & Horner, 1996), and effective behavior management strategies that meet these challenges and promote safety for students and adults are of significant interest for educators nationally. To confront these problems, many administrators have already successfully adopted school-wide intervention strategies to address concerns throughout the school environment. Most traditional behavior management programs have focused on teaching and rewarding appropriate student behaviors that typically occur in the classroom setting. While these strategies may be effective within the classroom, they often fail to address concerns associated with misbehavior in school common areas. School "common areas" can be described as places where relatively few adults supervise large groups of students, and little or no formalized instruction occurs — hallways, lunchrooms, playgrounds, and buses or bus lines. Previous research suggests that misbehavior in school common areas accounts for approximately one-half of all problem behaviors in many schools (Colvin, Sugai, Good, & Lee, 1997). In an assessment of office discipline referral frequency by location, 47% of all office-managed discipline referrals collected throughout the school year resulted from problems arising in common areas (Todd, Haugen, Anderson, & Spriggs, 2002). The average elementary school student with a thirty-minute lunch break, two ten-minute recesses, and occasional trips to and from the library may spend up to one hour or more of a typical school day in common areas. Therefore, given the amount of time students spend in common areas and the number of overall problem behaviors that reportedly occur there, it is estimated that  problem behavior is six times more likely to occur in common areas than in the classroom . Various circumstances have been identified as possible contributors: large numbers of students, a large amount of physical space to monitor, and too few adults trained to effectively deal with problem behaviors (Todd et al., 2002). The transition from structured classroom environments to unstructured common areas and back again several times throughout the school day may also pose a difficult task for many students. High-frequency transitions and shifting expectations across school common areas can lead to confusion that can inflate the number of problem behaviors. Lunchrooms, one of the most significant school common areas in regard to capacity and time of use, may be particularly subject to student misbehavior. Historically, inappropriate lunchroom behaviors have included talking while the aide is talking, being out of seat, and quarreling (MacPherson, Candee, & Hobman, 1974). In a survey conducted as part of a study by Samuels, Swerdlik, and Margolis (2001), common student complaints consisted of excessive noise level, students running and shouting, and lunchroom supervisors yelling at students; teacher concerns included confusion, messiness, and high noise level. Evidence also suggests that efforts to improve lunchroom behavior may lead to improvement in other aspects of the learning environment: in that same study, a decrease in inappropriate and disruptive lunchroom behaviors was accompanied by a decrease in office discipline referrals in the periods before and after lunch. Programs using positive methods of supporting appropriate behavior are highly effective in helping schools improve student behavior, for both individual students and groups of students, in common areas as well as in the classroom. These programs are consistent with research findings suggesting that the most effective programs for promoting lasting change focus on interventions implemented consistently across all school settings. One framework currently gaining momentum is Positive Behavior Support (PBS) as outlined by Carr et al. (2002). Because PBS is an approach rather than a set of specific programs and practices, there is considerable variability in the types of programs implemented at the school level; programs may fit the PBS theme but not necessarily be evidence-based. To improve quality and effectiveness, researchers should provide teachers and administrators with evidence-based guidelines: program intensity and coverage standards are needed, training procedures should be well documented, and data collection strategies should have planned interobserver reliability checks. Five evidence-based strategies behind the program Clear expectations and common language Defining rules and ensuring that students and teachers use common language to describe behaviors and consequences. Kartub et al. (2000) reduced hallway noise in a rural middle school by clarifying expectations and making hallways look different during transition times with small blinking lights: average decibel levels fell from 74.8, 76.5 and 76.8 (sixth, seventh, eighth grade) to 67.4, 68.6 and 68.9. Leedy, Bates, and Safran (2004) developed clear expectations schoolwide and saw a combined increase of 134.9% in appropriate student behavior in hallways. Contingent, specific praise Madsen, Becker, and Thomas (1968) modified teacher behavior to show the individual effects of rules, ignoring, and praise. Rules alone had little effect on problem behavior, ignoring produced inconsistent results, and ignoring accompanied by praise was very effective. The authors concluded that praise was the "key teacher behavior in achieving effective classroom management." Active supervision Defined by Colvin, Sugai, Good and Lee (1997) as "specific and overt behaviors (scanning, escorting, interacting) displayed by supervisors designed to prevent problem behavior and promote rule following behavior." In their demonstration in a rural elementary school of 475 students, staff were trained through explanation, demonstration and role-play, with twice-monthly reminders; problem behavior decreased across all transition areas and a significant correlation (−.83) was found between the number of student–teacher interactions and frequency of problem behavior. Token economies Token reinforcers are "symbolic representations exchangeable for some reinforcer of value to students" (Alberto & Troutman, 2003). They function like money: little inherent value, delivered immediately after the behavior, exchanged later for desired reinforcers. O'Leary, Becker, Evans and Saudargas (1969) found no consistent effects on behavior in any phase other than the token economy, where token reinforcement was associated with a significant reduction in problem behaviors. Differential reinforcement of incompatible behavior (DRI) A target behavior to be reduced is defined; then a behavior is chosen for increase that is mutually exclusive with it. If out-of-seat behavior is to be decreased, in-seat behavior is increased and reinforced. As the student is consistently reinforced for appropriate behavior, it increases and the problem behavior decreases (Alberto & Troutman, 2003). Zaghlawan, Ostrosky and Al-Khateeb (2007) used DRI with response cost to increase attentive behavior, with ANOVA results favoring the experimental group,  F (1,57) = 165.20,  p  < .0001. While there is an abundance of literature outlining specific programs and case studies utilizing these strategies, there is often little or no guidance available regarding best practice in their application. One example is the widely-used "good ticket" program: these systems are described as "Gotcha" coupons, "Chance" tickets, "High Fives," or "Pride tickets." In most instances these notes or tickets function as token reinforcers entered into a lottery or exchanged for rewards. There is a strong need for studies that outline minimum basic standards for program duration, intensity, tracking, and reinforcer delivery. Method Participants and setting Participants were approximately 200 first- through fifth-grade students in a rural northern Utah elementary school. The students were predominantly white (80%), and from middle to lower-middle socioeconomic backgrounds. The targeted setting was the school lunchroom, and all data collection took place during the regularly scheduled lunch period. Three grades were typically in the lunchroom at the same time (approximately 20 minutes for each grade), with younger grades rotating out as the older grades came in. The lunchroom was roughly divided into two sides: one with five rows of tables where students sat to eat, the other containing the lunch serving area, trashcans, and tray disposal counter. Students entered in lines through one of two entrances on the east wall, proceeded to the serving area, continued to a designated table, and exited through a door in the north wall after taking their trays to the disposal counter. Design and target behaviors This study employed a multiple baseline design (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 2006) across three targeted behaviors deemed inappropriate for the lunchroom by the school principal and faculty. Target behavior Definition Littering Leaving on the floor — all litter left on the tables was swept onto the floor by lunchroom staff — any object larger (length or width) than a 3×5 inch index card. Inappropriate sitting Standing while eating, or sitting with "back pockets off of the seat." Running Having both feet leave the floor at the same time. Procedure The Praise Note system was part of a school-wide effort to decrease problem behaviors and increase incompatible appropriate behaviors in the lunchroom. The principal, teachers, and lunchroom staff identified three target behaviors critical to student safety and to promoting a positive lunchroom environment. The intervention consisted of two components: (1) providing students and faculty with clear expectations for lunchroom behavior, and (2) implementing a Praise Note system to reward student behaviors meeting the expectations. Baseline.  During the baseline condition no programs were in place at the school to improve student behavior in the lunchroom. Lunchroom staff members circulated through the lunchroom correcting students at their own discretion. As no training had been provided concerning the delivery of praise statements, the rate of praise delivered to students during baseline was very low — in fact, the observers did not record any instances of praise statements happening during baseline. The Praise Note system.  Students, teachers, custodians, lunchroom staff, and school administrators all participated in training sessions. Afterwards, teachers and staff were instructed to reward students who displayed appropriate behaviors in the lunchroom by presenting them with a Praise Note, accompanied by specific, verbal praise. Praise Notes were small yellow slips of paper that contained student and teacher signature lines, the school mascot (an eagle), and the school motto ("safe, kind, and responsible"). To ensure that Praise Notes were always available, faculty members received blank Praise Notes in their boxes, notes were also available in the office, and the principal or custodian always had some in the lunchroom. Faculty members and administrators in the lunchroom were encouraged to deliver  one Praise Note every two to three minutes (VI 2.5 min) . What happened to a Praise Note 1 The teacher filled in the student's name and signed the Praise Note. 2 The student took the note to the office during the course of that school day. 3 Office staff provided a large decorated jar for the notes, and congratulated each student who put a note in the jar. 4 At the end of each school day the principal drew five Praise Notes and read the names over the intercom. 5 Those students went to the office and chose a small reward — pencil, eraser, folder, sticker — from a box in the principal's office. 6 To increase faculty participation, the teachers whose names were on the five selected notes were entered into a weekly drawing for a gift certificate or service voucher donated by local businesses. 7 After the drawing, all Praise Notes turned in were stapled to a large board in the main hallway near the school entrance. By filling the board, students worked collectively to earn a larger group reward — extra recess time, a party, or early lunch — after which the notes were taken down and the students began filling the board again. Training Teachers and other selected staff members (lunchroom personnel, custodians, and monitors) were given an overview of the program before the intervention began. They were taught when, how, and for which behaviors a Praise Note should be delivered. When delivering a note, staff were taught to state the student's name (or give some other initial positive interaction), carefully describe the behaviors for which the note was given, write the student's name on the note, and present it to the student. Staff were instructed to look for appropriate behaviors and deliver notes on a constant basis while in the lunchroom, and were encouraged to target students who were in need of extra help. Three training sessions were held, one focusing on each of the three target behaviors, conducted for all students and participating faculty the day prior to the beginning of each phase. Classes were brought into the lunchroom for a four-part session lasting approximately 20 minutes: an introduction and three learning stations of about 5 minutes each. Introduction.  The new lunchroom expectations were introduced with explicit definitions of what behaviors were and were not appropriate, including examples and non-examples. Students were introduced to the Praise Note system and told how they could earn notes. They were told they would not receive a Praise Note every time they were acting appropriately, but that consistently meeting expectations would increase their chances. They were also told to deliver notes to the office for the daily drawing, after which the notes would be posted on the hallway board toward a group reward such as an ice cream party or extra recess. Station one A trainer reviewed the information from the introduction and clarified expectations by allowing students to ask questions. The trainer also used a game: tossing a beanbag to students, with the student who caught it given a hypothetical situation and asked to determine if the student in the situation was eligible to receive a Praise Note. Station two Students demonstrated the target behaviors in a fun and positive way; the content differed with each training.  Running:  a walking relay — if both feet left the ground the student went back to the beginning and tried again.  Littering:  a relay picking up a tray with a napkin and paper strips, walking to the trash can without spilling, dumping the contents, stacking trays neatly, and tagging the next student.  Sitting:  a game in which students lined up, walked past the serving area, sat down single file, filled the benches, kept "pockets on the seat" until all were seated, then practiced exiting correctly, with the trainer timing each round as students tried to beat their previous time. Station three Students practiced the appropriate behaviors and answered questions about when a Praise Note would be given. As each student successfully demonstrated the appropriate behavior, he or she received a Praise Note — each student received at least one during this exercise — with the reminder that consistent appropriate behavior increases the likelihood of earning one. Measurement All observations were conducted during the regularly scheduled lunch period, which began at 11:55 a.m., when the first grade entered, and ended at 12:45 p.m. The daily observation period lasted from 11:55 a.m. to 12:32 p.m. Because the lunch schedule rotated and the number of students in the room varied, the number of behaviors occurring throughout the observation period fluctuated; therefore, frequency of behavior over the entire lunch period was used as the dependent measure. Littering.  Any object left on the floor larger than a 3×5 inch index card. This allowed for the inclusion of napkins, straw wrappers and milk jugs while excluding crumbs and wrappers torn into many small pieces — one student shredding a napkin should not be counted as several instances. Before the lunch period, observers confirmed there was no litter on the floor; afterwards, they walked around the lunchroom and counted the pieces left. Inappropriate sitting.  Standing while eating or sitting with "back pockets off of the seat," accounting for students who stood up or walked around, turned around in seats, and hung off benches. Students were not included until after they had received their tray, placed it on the table, and sat down, and were excluded after the tray was removed. Observers stood at the head of each table, switching tables every 30 seconds, quickly scanning and counting students sitting inappropriately using a manual hand-held counter — allowing each table to be counted once every 2.5 minutes. Running.  Both feet leaving the floor at the same time within the observation area, which included hopping, skipping and jumping. Boundaries were set near both cafeteria entrances and extended 30 feet into the cafeteria. Two independent observers, one near each line, recorded instances using a two-column data collection sheet with time in two-minute increments; totals were added at the end of each session to yield a daily total. Results Daily totals of inappropriate behavior for each condition were plotted and visually analyzed for within- and between-phase differences. Target behavior Baseline average Intervention average Decrease Litter (pieces) 34.3 1.3 96% Inappropriate sitting (instances) 65.5 23.3 65% Running (instances) 34 8.5 75% Interobserver agreement.  In all conditions a second observer, following the same protocol as the primary observer, conducted agreement checks. For littering, checks were taken across 43% of the total data collection sessions and averaged 98% agreement. For inappropriate sitting, checks were taken across 28% of sessions and averaged 90% agreement. For running, the additional observer was stationed on top of the bleachers where both lines were visible; checks were conducted on 28% of trials and averaged 87% agreement. Percent agreement was calculated by dividing the two frequency totals (smaller/larger) and multiplying by 100. Procedural integrity.  Data were taken on 61% of the observation days by the primary lunchroom observer, who randomly chose two lunchroom staff members and checked that (1) a Praise Note was delivered at least one time during a three-minute period, (2) the praise procedure was followed as outlined in the training, and (3) the note was filled out correctly. Staff met expectations on 100% of the observations, and there were no instances where it was necessary to retrain the delivery procedures. Discussion and conclusions The data demonstrate that the Praise Note system provides a successful method for decreasing inappropriate behaviors in an elementary school lunchroom. The authors believe the program's success can be attributed to the incorporation of several evidence-based strategies: establishing a common language to communicate behavioral expectations through direct teaching and posted signs; the delivery of praise as a social reinforcer; active supervision, with school personnel consistently moving around the lunchroom and interacting with students; Praise Notes functioning as token reinforcers delivered immediately and exchanged for other reinforcers later; and the principles of DRI, by selectively reinforcing positive behaviors incompatible with the negative target behaviors. This collection of strategies, implemented as a complete program, was critical to achieving the outcomes documented. Limitations One limitation is the inability to isolate the impact of each component of the Praise Note system on the target behaviors. This precludes any recommendation regarding which strategies could be separated and used as a stand-alone intervention, although many of the cited studies demonstrate the effectiveness of these strategies in other settings. Future research could systematically investigate which components yield the greatest impact. The study also does not provide evidence of the intervention's impact on appropriate student behaviors. It can be inferred that appropriate behaviors — sitting quietly, walking, not littering — increased, but data were not collected to directly substantiate this claim. Anecdotal evidence, in the form of a short survey collected from teachers and lunchroom staff, suggests that improved student–adult relationships were a positive side effect. The authors suspect that the unique delivery method may have contributed to these positive outcomes: when delivering a note, staff provided individualized, specific praise in addition to the tangible note, ensuring that each student who received one — even those whose names were not drawn — received recognition and had a positive interaction with school personnel. The principal, lunchroom monitors, custodian and regular lunchroom staff regularly made positive comments about specific students whose behavior had improved, and general statements about the improved overall attitude in the lunchroom and students' willingness to encourage peers to behave appropriately. Implications for practitioners Intensity.  Because the number of Praise Notes delivered was not systematically varied, the optimal intensity cannot be stated. However, over the course of the study and throughout the rest of the school year the number of notes delivered in the lunchroom averaged  110 per week , meaning that approximately 55% of students received a Praise Note each week. Lunchroom staff reported that this number did not seem unreasonable, especially since they were eager to have a method for rewarding students. The teacher reinforcement component was also likely a factor in maintaining a high, steady rate of delivery. This intensity was sufficient to show definite change in all three target behaviors; less intense interventions may show similar results, but further research is necessary. Variety of reinforcers.  Programs may enjoy increased success if multiple types of reinforcers are used. The reinforcers in this study included social reinforcers (teacher praise and office staff recognition), token reinforcers (tickets), public posting (notes on the hallway board), group rewards (parties and extra recess), and tangibles (erasers, pencils, folders). This program presents a method for schools to provide a variety of reinforcers in a practical manner.
